transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-05-14 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jon Ramos (Redwood SE), Liam Holloway (CTO - Holloway Logistics), Priya Singh (Platform Engineer), Marcus Bell (SRE), Gina Torres (Procurement)

Summary (auto): Discussed reliability expectations and pilot acceptance criteria; compared Hosted, Dedicated, Private; sketched fallback strategy and rollout plan.

00:00 Maya Patel: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, um I'll kick off — I'm Maya, AE on the account, and this is Jon our SE. We're looking forward to hearing your constraints for reliability and what a successful pilot looks like.
00:22 Liam Holloway: Yeah thanks Maya. Quick context — Holloway runs global logistics routing, most traffic is US/EU, about 35% of our requests must remain EU-resident for customers in Germany and France. We're exploring Redwood because we need predictable latency and an SLO we can commit to.
00:45 Jon Ramos: Great, thanks Liam. Can you share target SLOs? Are you thinking 99.9 uptime, and what latency p95/p99 targets?
00:56 Liam Holloway: Ideally 99.95 uptime for core API, p95 under 450ms for our small routing prompts, p99 under 1s. But we know those are tight if you add a bunch of tokens and long context. So we want to discuss fallbacks — like routing to a smaller model or cached answers instead of returning an error.
01:18 Priya Singh: Also, curious about multi-region routing. If EU region has transient infra issues, what does Redwood do? Will traffic automatically steer to US region? Our compliance folks are worried about that because of data residency.
01:34 Jon Ramos: Good question. For Hosted we support routing policies with region restrictions — you can pin model variants to regions; we also support failover rules. Default behavior is to not cross region unless you configure a fallback policy that allows EU->non-EU failover. For Dedicated and Private you can set the policy at the cluster level.
01:54 Marcus Bell: So if it's a burst in EU capacity, can we have a degraded mode where the request fails over to a smaller quantized model in EU first, then only cross to US if EU capacity is exhausted?
02:09 Jon Ramos: Yes. We commonly implement an ordered fallback chain: primary model (full FP16 model) in region; fallback to quantized variant in same region; fallback to regional cache returns; final fallback to a lower-cost hosted model or queued response. That sequence minimizes cross-border exposure.
02:30 Liam Holloway: That sounds promising. Important — we need audit logs for any cross-region fallback events and a way to flag them for our compliance team.
02:40 Maya Patel: Absolutely — audit logs and explicit policy events are part of our Console. We'll surface fallback events, timestamps, and the triggering error (e.g., capacity, kernel OOM, throttling).
02:55 Gina Torres: Procurement question — if we go Dedicated reserved, what do SLAs look like? And what's the remedy if the SLA is missed?
03:05 Maya Patel: For Dedicated we offer financial credits tied to monthly availability thresholds; we can discuss the exact numbers in the SOW. For Hosted our standard terms are lower availability guarantees but with faster onboarding.
03:20 Priya Singh: We also need KMS integration and HSM support. We cannot have keys residing outside our cloud. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS and provide customer-managed keys for embeddings and logs?
03:35 Jon Ramos: Yes. Private and Dedicated support customer KMS integration, and for Private we can integrate with on-prem HSM. For Hosted we offer bring-your-own-KMS for encryption at rest for certain customers — we'd need to map the exact flows and see if your case requires HSM-backed signing.
03:55 Marcus Bell: What about rollout behavior? If we do a canary, what does observability give us? We need token-level latency and error breakdowns, and a way to automatically rollback if p99 doubles.
04:12 Jon Ramos: Console provides per-route token latency histograms, error rates, and you can set automated rollback thresholds. Example: canary 5% of traffic, watch 15m window, if p99(latency) > 2x baseline or errors > 0.5% we auto-roll back. Those thresholds are configurable.
04:36 Liam Holloway: On the pilot acceptance criteria — what would you expect? We want a list so our execs can sign off.
04:44 Maya Patel: Typical pilot acceptance includes: 1) Latency & availability baseline for a 48h synthetic and 24h production shadow test; 2) Successful execution of fallback chain under induced failure (simulate zone outage); 3) Audit logs visible to customer; 4) KMS/HSM connectivity test; 5) Runbook handoff and a successful checklist for oncall.
05:06 Priya Singh: For the simulated failure, you mean we'll purposely throttle the EU cluster and observe failover to quantized model, then if that saturates, see region steering?
05:17 Jon Ramos: Exactly. We'll run a staged chaos test in a test namespace — start with load increase, then OOM/slot drain, then disable the EU cluster to validate regional steering. We'll produce artifacts: graphs, logs, and a replayable test plan.
05:33 Liam Holloway: So what about cost tradeoffs? Hot-standby across EU+US is expensive. Could we accept some degree of graceful degradation where non-critical calls return a cached or summarised response instead of failing?
05:47 Maya Patel: Yes, that's often the pragmatic approach — tier your routes. Critical routing requests go to high-SLA Dedicated pools; background analytics can be routed to cheaper hosted or queued. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and quantization to reduce cost for hotspots.
06:05 Marcus Bell: A practical question — how do we instrument for the SLA? Do you emit SLO metrics we can pull into our Prometheus?
06:13 Jon Ramos: We expose metrics and traces via integrations (Prometheus, Datadog). We also provide token-level breakdowns in Console and can stream raw events to your SIEM for retention.
06:28 Gina Torres: From procurement perspective, can we start with a time-boxed pilot with a not-to-exceed cost? We need to signest a PO (purchase order) and not open-ended spend.
06:38 Maya Patel: Yes, we can structure a pilot SOW with a capped commitment for the pilot period (eg 30 days) and define acceptance criteria. If you move to Dedicated, we can credit pilot spend against committed reserved capacity.
06:51 Priya Singh: One more on private deployments — our infra team often runs air-gapped clusters. Is Redwood Private available as an on-prem package and what's the upgrade cadence?
07:02 Jon Ramos: There's an on-prem package for Private that runs in air-gapped environments. Upgrade cadence is part of the enterprise plan — we usually schedule quarterly patch windows but can do more frequent security patches on request.
07:18 Liam Holloway: For the audit side, must confirm SOC2 and ISO docs. Also need evidence of periodic penetration tests.
07:26 Maya Patel: We have a standard security pack (SOC2 Type II attestation, ISO certs where applicable), and can share recent pentest summaries under NDA. We'll include that in the security packet.
07:38 Marcus Bell: During the pilot, if we see sustained degradation, who is oncall from Redwood? How does escalation work?
07:46 Jon Ramos: During pilot we provide SE oncall during business hours and a follow-the-sun pager for enterprise pilots. For Dedicated with premium SLA we include 24/7 escalation paths. We'll include those contacts in the SOW.
08:01 Liam Holloway: Good. Can we get an example of a fallback policy config? A concrete YAML or console screenshot would help our infra team review.
08:10 Jon Ramos: Yep — action item: I'll send the fallback policy examples and a sample runbook. They show sequencing, thresholds, and metadata emitted to logs.
08:22 Gina Torres: Timeline — procurement wants pilot to start by May 29 so finance can close the quarter. Any blockers?
08:30 Maya Patel: We can hit that if we finalize SOW this week and get PO. We'll scope a 30-day pilot starting 2028-05-29.
08:38 Liam Holloway: Okay good. One more nuance — for EU customers we may need local data processors. Does Redwood allow per-customer data routing so EU-origin stays within EU?
08:50 Jon Ramos: Yes — routing policies can be per-api-key or per-tenant. We can ensure EU-origin tokens hit EU clusters and that logs are retained in region. For anything that crosses boundary we'll record the event.
09:05 Priya Singh: That helps. Also can you surface KV cache hits/miss rates in the dashboard? We'd like to track cache effectiveness because it affects latency and cost.
09:14 Jon Ramos: KV cache metrics are exposed — hit rates, cache priming suggestions are shown in Optimize. We can also push raw cache telemetry to your observability stack.
09:28 Liam Holloway: Perfect. For the pilot acceptance demonstration, we want a runbook doc, a short chaos test, and a failure artifacts pack. Will Redwood run the chaos test or do we?
09:38 Jon Ramos: We can run it jointly — we'll run the scenario in partnership with your SREs and provide step-by-step scripts.
09:46 Maya Patel: Quick recap and next steps: Maya to send pricing and SOW; Jon to send fallback YAML, runbook template, and baseline benchmark plan; Liam to share EU residency numbers and security contact details; target pilot kickoff week of May 29.
09:58 Liam Holloway: Sounds good. Thanks all.
10:02 Gina Torres: We'll review SOW and try to get PO in by Friday.
10:08 Maya Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the packet and proposed SOW.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-words — e.g., "Red Wood Dedicated" appears in some ASR lines; acronyms like K V cache sometimes split; filler words kept for authenticity.
